entries.title: Exposure to relational information pollution in social media and mental health among adolescents and young adults
entries.abstract: Drawing from the literature on information pollution, we explored whether exposure to polluted content about users' social environment might influence users’ mental health. To achieve this goal, we proposed the term “relational information pollution” to describe the extent to which users are exposed to harmful, polluted content about their social environment on social media. The working hypothesis of this study was that exposure to relational information pollution on social media is associated with higher depressive symptoms among adolescents and young adults. Multivariate linear regression and multiple-group analyses across gender and age-group models were conducted using data from a nationally representative survey of 1002 adolescent and young adult participants aged 14 to 18 years from the Spanish population. Relational information pollution showed a significant positive association with depressive symptoms (β = .08, p < .01) after accounting for different personality characteristics, social media use mindsets (i.e., agency and valence), digital stress (i.e., social pressure or availability stress, approval anxiety, and FoMO), social support, sociodemographic characteristics (gender, age, and studying status at the time of the survey), frequency of social media use, and systematic response bias (social desirability and presence of parents or legal guardians during the completion of the questionnaire). Multiple-group analyses indicated equivalence in results between boys and girls, as well as between younger and older participants, suggesting that the association between relational information pollution and depressive symptoms transcends gender and age demographics. Exposure to relational information pollution on social media is pervasive among adolescents and young adults and is associated with increased depressive symptoms.

entries.title: A National Pediatric Primary Care Research Agenda
entries.abstract: Pediatric primary care (PPC) promotes child wellbeing through health supervision, anticipatory guidance, screening, and intervention. Given an evolving PPC landscape, content experts collaborated with the American Academy of Pediatrics Pediatric Research in Office Settings network in an iterative, multiyear process to create a PPC research agenda to advance child health that reflects professional and family priorities. Using an adapted nominal group technique, we identified research areas of focus based on (1) what PPC clinicians said they frequently encounter in practice; (2) the extent of the problem for families nationally; (3) evidence gaps; and (4) areas in which research could have the highest impact on child health. From 2022 to 2024, we synthesized contributor feedback from 8 key content expert sessions. This process resulted in 6 interconnected domains of highest priority for PPC research: (1) child mental health, (2) obesity, (3) communicating science to support families, (4) pediatric workforce, (5) injury prevention, and (6) adolescent health. We identified cross-cutting themes that warrant research in connection with these 6 prioritized domains. Examples of such themes include removing barriers to access and ensuring quality services for all children; under-resourced communities; care coordination and linkages within and outside PPC; supporting parents/caregivers; and technology and social media, which can serve as tools to enhance practice and can be assets or threats to child wellbeing. This manuscript details a vision for a national, coordinated PPC research agenda to inform investigators' and funders' efforts to advance primary health care and the health of all children based on our results.
